quests.definition: 'Warm up to someone' means to gradually develop positive feelings toward them.
quests.example: The dog was shy at first but slowly warmed up to the new neighbor.
quests.exampleSentence: The dog was shy at first but slowly warmed up to the new neighbor.
quests.contextSentence: The dog was shy at first but slowly warmed up to the new neighbor.
quests.origin: A literal temperature metaphor, part of the same family as 'break the ice' and 'the cold shoulder,' using warmth for friendliness.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: The word-for-word physical action | Figurative: Warm up to someone means to gradually develop positive feelings toward them.
quests.nativeTip: Native speakers use "WARM UP TO SOMEONE" informally. Pair it with conversational tone.

quests.definition: 'Jump to conclusions' means to form a judgment before having enough information.
quests.example: Don't jump to conclusions — maybe they were planning your birthday.

quests.conceptTitle: Idiom Anatomy: BARK UP THE WRONG TREE
quests.definition: 'Bark up the wrong tree' fits a specific mistaken accusation about who or what caused something, while 'jump to conclusions' is the broader idiom for deciding too quickly in general.
quests.example: If you think I broke it, you're barking up the wrong tree.
quests.exampleSentence: If you think I broke it, you're barking up the wrong tree.
quests.contextSentence: If you think I broke it, you're barking up the wrong tree.
quests.origin: See the earlier note on 'bark up the wrong tree' — from hunting dogs barking at the wrong tree after losing track of their prey.

quests.conceptTitle: Idiom Anatomy: BE QUICK TO JUDGE
quests.definition: 'Be quick to judge' means to criticize or form opinions about someone too fast, often unfairly.
quests.example: Try not to be so quick to judge — you don't know her whole situation.
quests.exampleSentence: Try not to be so quick to judge — you don't know her whole situation.
quests.contextSentence: Try not to be so quick to judge — you don't know her whole situation.
quests.origin: A plain, transparent phrase describing hasty moral evaluation, distinct from the more specific 'jump to conclusions,' which covers any hasty judgment, not just critical ones.

quests.definition: 'Take something personally' means to interpret a general or neutral comment as a direct insult.
quests.example: He didn't mean it as an attack — try not to take it personally.

quests.word: HAVE A CHIP ON YOUR SHOULDER
quests.conceptTitle: Idiom Anatomy: HAVE A CHIP ON YOUR SHOULDER
quests.definition: 'Have a chip on your shoulder' means to carry constant resentment or a defensive attitude, often stemming from a past slight.
quests.example: Ever since he was passed over for the promotion, he's had a chip on his shoulder.
quests.exampleSentence: Ever since he was passed over for the promotion, he's had a chip on his shoulder.
quests.contextSentence: Ever since he was passed over for the promotion, he's had a chip on his shoulder.
quests.origin: Believed to come from a 19th-century American custom where a person would balance a wood chip on their shoulder, daring anyone to knock it off and start a fight.
